arguments.prompt:
The user now authorizes a NEW compact-hexagon simulation and resulting map with a CHANGED TERMINATION RULE ONLY. Please actually execute the fresh simulation; do not just redisplay an old checkpoint that happens to pass.

Agreed stopping rule after each complete round:
For each hexagonal SERVICE REGION i with load Li and each neighbor j sharing a positive-length boundary INSIDE the authoritative Manhattan main-island domain, compute gij=100*abs(Li-Lj)/Li. Its local score mi is the MEDIAN of its neighbor gaps. The global score M is the MEDIAN of all 38 local scores. Stop after the FIRST full round with M<=5%. Standard median averages the two middle values for even counts. A zero-load cell adjacent to any positive-load neighbor has local score +infinity (explicitly assigned at cell level); a zero-load cell with only zero-load neighbors has score zero. Do not drop empty cells from the global median. Every region should have a neighbor; treat an isolated positive-area cell as a geometry defect. This is termination only: do NOT replace the existing load-balance objective or movement acceptance with median improvement. No zero-movement requirement and no insistence that every cell reach +/-10%.

Keep previous local shared-corner/coordinated-neighbor proposals, existing balance-improvement/local-annealing acceptance, convex six-sided UNDERLYING cells, no overlaps and full authoritative-island coverage. Width ratio <=2 on BOTH underlying hexagons and actual clipped service regions. Use a valid FEASIBLE initial 38-cell mesh on the authoritative NYC DCP 26b main-island geometry verified last turn. The historical map re-clipped to that domain was NOT feasible (gap .017135 km2, clipped ratio2.23311), so repair geometry before counting simulation rounds; verify and report initial metrics. Do not silently start from the old nearly balanced checkpoint: use original regular 38-cell initialization plus geometry repair, as in the earlier compactness experiment. Report exact baseline/seed and whether initial repaired state already passes M<=5%; if so still execute at least one full round as requested, recording that fact.

Retain all 5,986 records in reporting; three known records (indices309,4705,5212) outside official land remain marked and excluded from service-region ownership exactly as the verified map (5,983 inside). Do not snap, buffer or silently discard them. Use recovered coordinate transform and authoritative full-resolution boundary for checks. The earlier impossibility for EVERY cell within +/-10% is irrelevant under this median criterion; do not stop because of that old certificate.

At termination give executed round count, initial/final M, all 38 counts/neighbor lists/local medians, maximum underlying/clipped width ratio, coverage residual, overlap area and unique assignment count. Call failures/incomplete runs honestly; do not call time caps success. Save reproducible geometry/code/metrics.

MOST IMPORTANT: return a compact machine-readable JSON or complete SVG <=18,000 characters so the resulting NEW map can be displayed HERE. Prefer JSON with ordered 6-vertex coordinates of each cell, actual clipped centroid for labels, counts, and original-mesh plus actual-service adjacency. I already have the simplified official main-island outline including its hole from your previous SVG, and the km transform, so you need not resend the long shoreline; reuse EXACT same authoritative dataset/frame. Include stage=new_median_termination_result and data checks to prevent confusing it with the old inspection-only map. Create your own PNG/PDF too if useful, but opaque content-reference links alone cannot transfer the map. Please execute and show the new result now.

content.text: but indeed median and not average?

items.text:
Yes, **median**, not average—at both levels:

1. Each hexagon takes the **median** of its percentage gaps to neighbors.
2. The stopping score is the **median** of those hexagon scores.

Current score: **0.88%**. Proposed stopping threshold: **≤5%**.

content.text: ok, we are looking at a termination rule, not acceptance criteria.  So let's use the median as the termination rule, what should it be?

items.text: I’d start with a 5% threshold on the median across all hexagons. I’ll check the current value with the empty cell included.

I suggest: **stop after a full round when the median of all hexagons’ median neighbor gaps is ≤5%.**

This changes only termination; the movement and acceptance rules stay unchanged.

Count an empty cell bordering a nonempty one as having an infinite gap. Including it, the current overall median is **0.88%**, so this result already qualifies.

This deliberately tolerates outliers; it does not require every hexagon to be balanced.

content.text: ok, do the median gap, tell me the result

items.text: I’ll replace the sum with the median neighbor gap, keeping each hexagon’s own load as the percentage base.

Using the **median percentage gap to neighbors for each hexagon**:

- **Median across the 37 nonempty hexagons:** **0.58%**.
- **Worst hexagon’s median gap:** **1,158.3%**—the 6-pickup cell bordering loads 139 and 0.
- The empty hexagon remains undefined because its percentage base is zero.

So most cells are locally well balanced; the northern tip remains the outlier.

content.text: fyou calculate it for each hexagon as the basis, and all its neighbours

items.text:
Understood: **each hexagon’s own load is the percentage base**.

\[
S_h=100\sum_{j\text{ neighboring }h}\frac{|L_h-L_j|}{L_h}.
\]

For the **6-pickup hexagon**, with neighbors holding **139 and 0**:

\[
S_h=100\frac{133+6}{6}=\mathbf{2316.7\%}.
\]

That is the **largest score among nonempty hexagons** in the displayed map.

The **empty hexagon’s score is undefined**, because its own load is zero. We still need a convention for that case before this can serve as a stopping rule for every hexagon.

content.text: this is really good, let's try with a different, local termination rule, that the sum of differences of percentages of loads among a hexagon and its neighbours is not more than X%.  please calculate this number of the current result

items.text: I’ll calculate this from the displayed map, using shared-edge neighbors and absolute load differences so positive and negative differences cannot cancel. The largest cell score will give the smallest X that lets every cell stop.

How should each load difference be expressed as a percentage? For loads 100 and 150, these choices give different scores.
- Relative to the pair’s average: 40% (symmetric and handles an empty cell)
- Relative to the cell’s own load: 50% from the 100-load cell
- As shares of all pickups: difference in percentage points

items.text:
Understood—no more multiple-choice forms.

For a local rule, I’d express each difference **relative to the two cells’ average load**. Loads of 100 and 150 then differ by 40%, whichever cell calculates it.

Using that definition, and neighbors sharing a border **inside Manhattan**, the current worst sum is **383.4%**:

- The cell with **6 pickups** borders cells with **139** and **0**.
- Its differences are **183.4% + 200%**.

But this exposes an important issue: **0 versus 6 counts as a larger percentage difference than 100 versus 150**.

How would you want those two situations to compare? That determines a useful meaning for your local stopping rule.

items.text: The best compact partition kept every width ratio below 2:1 and preserved coverage, but loads ranged from 0 to 181 pickups. For comparison, the earlier balanced solution had ratios above 11:1—consistent with the elongated shapes you objected to.

**Tested: compact cells are achievable, but this run did not reach full load balance.**

On all 5,986 pickups, using 38 cells:

| | Earlier balanced solution | Compactness-constrained |
|---|---:|---:|
| Worst width ratio | 11.2:1 | **2:1** |
| Pickups per cell | 157–158 | 0–181 |
| Cells within ±10% | 38/38 | **32/38** |

The compact solution preserved coverage, convex hexagons, and no overlaps.

**The main difficulty is the sparsely populated northern tip.** Under the modeled outline, a region covering that tip cannot contain the required 142 pickups while satisfying 2:1 compactness.

However, I found that the simulator’s outline was labeled **“for orientation only.”** So this establishes a limitation of that approximate model, not necessarily real Manhattan.

**I’d verify the geographic boundary before relaxing the compactness constraint.**
